say: You give it two sides of a triangle and the **angle** between them, or all three sides. It finds the missing side or angle.
The key idea: the cosine rule is Pythagoras with a correction. It works in any triangle, not just a right-angled one.
what.in: two sides + angle between, or three sides

how.higher: Higher level uses it almost every year on Paper 2, usually as one step in a longer question, and as a part of its own worth 10 marks.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 2 nearly every year, often as a part of its own worth 5 to 15 marks, inside a question about a field, a boat or a map.

example.question: In triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = 9$ cm, $|AC| = 12$ cm and $|\angle BAC| = 40^\circ$. Find $|BC|$, correct to two decimal places.

steps.title: Write the cosine rule
steps.say: You know two sides and the angle between them. Use the cosine rule with $a = |BC|$ opposite the $\hl{1}{40^\circ}$ angle.

lines.text: Check your calculator is in degree mode.

steps.title: Work out a squared
steps.say: Multiply, then subtract. Do not take the square root yet.

steps.title: Take the square root
steps.say: Square root both sides to get the side $a$.

Substitute fully into the formula. A correct, fully substituted formula earns High Partial Credit.

say: You give it a shape made of several triangles, such as a field split by a diagonal. It finds the lengths, angles and **areas** one triangle at a time.
The key idea: the answer from one triangle becomes the input to the next. Start with the triangle where you know enough.

how.higher: Higher level uses it as a step inside Paper 2 questions about flights and distances, 10 marks for the part that chains the sine or cosine rule.

example.question: A field $ABCD$ is split by the diagonal $[AC]$. In triangle $ABC$, $|AB| = 7$ m, $|BC| = 9$ m and $|\angle ABC| = 70^\circ$. In triangle $ACD$, $|CD| = 8$ m and $|\angle ACD| = 50^\circ$. Find the area of the field, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the diagonal
steps.say: Triangle $ABC$ has two sides and the angle between them. Use the cosine rule to find $\hl{1}{|AC|}$, which both triangles share.

steps.title: Area of triangle ABC
steps.say: Use the area formula with two sides and the angle between them.

steps.title: Area of triangle ACD
steps.say: Now use the diagonal $\hl{1}{9.32}$ with $|CD|$ and the angle between them.

steps.title: Add the two areas
steps.say: The field is the two triangles together.

lines.text: To one decimal place, that is $58.2$ m$^2$.

higher.tip: Write the sine or cosine rule with some substitution. That alone earns Low Partial Credit.

sources.quote: sine rule or cosine rule stated with some substitution
Sine rule formulated with some substitution

higher.tip: A rule with full substitution earns Mid Partial Credit, even if you do not finish.

sources.quote: sine rule or cosine rule with full substitution

say: You give it two sides and an angle that is **not** between them. It finds the angle you want, and checks whether there are two triangles.
The key idea: $\sin \theta$ has two angles between $0^\circ$ and $180^\circ$. If the second one still fits in the triangle, both answers count.

how.higher: Higher level has asked for it once, on Paper 2 in 2024, as a 10 mark part where both angles had to be given.

example.question: In triangle $ABC$, $|BC| = 10$ cm, $|AC| = 13$ cm and $|\angle BAC| = 35^\circ$. Find the two possible values of $|\angle ABC|$, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Use the sine rule
steps.say: Match each side with the angle opposite it. $|BC|$ is opposite $35^\circ$, and $|AC|$ is opposite the angle $B$ we want.

steps.title: Find sin B
steps.say: Multiply both sides by $13$ to get $\hl{1}{\sin B}$ on its own.

steps.title: Find the first angle
steps.say: Take the inverse sine for the angle in the first quadrant.

steps.title: Find the second angle
steps.say: The sine is positive in the second quadrant too. Subtract from $180^\circ$. Check that it still fits: $131.8^\circ + 35^\circ < 180^\circ$.

higher.tip: Give the angle from the second quadrant as well. The scheme expects both, and one angle earns only partial credit.
Write the sine rule with the numbers put in. A fully substituted sine rule earns Mid Partial Credit.

sources.quote: Sine rule with fully correct substitution

higher.tip: Round at the end, to the accuracy the question asks for. Wrong rounding costs a mark.

sources.quote: Apply a * if not rounded correctly

say: You give it a solid, such as a box, a pyramid or a mast with wires. It finds a length or an **angle** inside it.
The key idea: pick out a flat triangle, usually right-angled, that contains what you want. Then use Pythagoras, trigonometry, or the sine or cosine rule on it.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 2 in some years, as a part worth 10 to 15 marks that chains Pythagoras with a trigonometry or cosine rule step.

example.question: A box has a rectangular base $12$ cm by $5$ cm and a height of $6$ cm. Find the angle between a space diagonal and the base, correct to one decimal place.

steps.title: Find the base diagonal
steps.say: The space diagonal, the base diagonal and the vertical edge form a right-angled triangle. First find the $\hl{1}{\text{base diagonal}}$ with Pythagoras.

steps.title: Pick the right triangle
steps.say: The angle $\theta$ is between the space diagonal and its shadow on the base. The shadow is $\hl{1}{13}$. The side opposite $\theta$ is the height, $6$.

steps.title: Use tan
steps.say: We know the opposite and adjacent sides, so use tan.

higher.tip: Show the Pythagoras step for each flat diagonal. Marks are given for finding the lengths on the way.

sources.quote: Work of merit in both parts

higher.tip: Write the length of any diagonal as soon as you can. It earns Low Partial Credit.
A fully substituted cosine rule earns High Partial Credit in a 3D problem.
Put the unit on every length. A missing or wrong unit costs a mark.
